lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Opening day. You're opening-day lead this morning, so the calls are yours.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: First topic: Siti texted at quarter to seven, her kid's in hospital, so we're one short for the 8 to 10 rush.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The free-kopi flyers went to every office in the building, about 200 of them, so the whole building is coming at 8.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: Auntie Mary is on her rest day. Asking her in means double pay, and she can say no.

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: Anyone new on the till needs a login, and that takes me about 15 minutes before 8.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So how do we run the counter from 8 to 10 one person short?

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: A manager could cover, but whoever it is drops their own opening-day job.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Going quiet on the free kopi now would be worse. The whole building has the flyer.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Noted. Who covers the counter if Auntie Mary says no?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Next topic: the old regulars and the new kopi prices.

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.text: Kopi was $1.30 here and the new menu charges $2.40. Photos of the old regulars hang on the wall.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: On this rent a cup costs us about $1.60, so the old price loses money on every cup.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The nephew's post has about 300 shares, and the food blogger reads the local Facebook groups.

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: The till can take a regulars' price button in about 10 minutes, but it needs a rule for who gets it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What do we do for the old regulars without losing money on every cup?

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.text: We could hold the price and explain it at the counter, with a reply on Facebook.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: Then someone has to decide who counts as a regular before the till button means anything.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Mei, can you draft the regulars' note for the counter and Facebook?

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.text: Yes, I'll draft the regulars' note, and we can settle the rule for the till button.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Next: laptop campers and the breakfast seat crunch.

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: The booth sockets share one timer switch, and the Wi-Fi can give each receipt a code that lasts 45 minutes.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: The blocked seats cost us real breakfast sales at the trial, about $420.

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.text: Most morning customers come alone with a hot tray, and we have 10 window-bar stools in the storeroom.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: 9 of 16 laptop users wore upstairs lanyards, and two of those offices have asked about bulk orders.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How do we free up seats without anyone having to confront customers?

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: A laptop zone on the window stools and breakfast-table signs would do it without staff stepping in.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Arjun, can you set the booth socket timer before 8?

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: Yes, I'll set the booth socket timer, and I'll test the Wi-Fi codes before opening.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Next: food safety. The inspector's routine check is at 9.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: The night cleaner unplugged the prep fridge after the trial and it was off about three hours last night. The head chef found it at 6:10 and signed the disposal log.

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.text: The eggs and kaya are gone until the 10 o'clock delivery, and Set A is about 40% of breakfast sales.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The customer's email is polite, but she says she will post her review tonight. The blogger comes at 10:30.

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: The fridge has no alarm. A temperature alert on the POS takes me 10 minutes, and I was asked for one last month.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Do we open at 8, and what do we tell the customer and the inspector?

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: We open at 8 without Set A until the delivery, and we give the officer both logs.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I'll answer the customer before her review goes up.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Wei Ling, can you email the customer and attach both logs?

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: Yes, I'll email the customer and attach both logs, and cover the $85 clinic bill.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Last topic: the delivery app commission squeeze.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: GrabFood's promo rate on its cut for all our shops ended today, and we lose about 50 cents on each $10 breakfast set delivered.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: A delivered set costs $7.30, while a five-set platter costs only $29 because the packaging is shared.

lines.speaker: Arjun
lines.text: GrabFood hides shops that charge more on the app than at the counter, and an app menu change takes 15 minutes.

lines.speaker: Mei
lines.text: Platters need the large trays, and we have 30.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How do we stop losing money on delivery without losing the office customers?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Most office orders are five sets or more, and 12 office managers have asked for a direct code.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: Then the platters and the pickup code are worth pricing properly before the rush.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Daniel, can you email GrabFood to confirm the platter listing and the pickup code?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Yes, I'll email GrabFood to confirm the platter listing, and I'll send the pickup code to the offices.

lines.speaker: Wei Ling
lines.text: I'll post the final plan in the team channel once we settle the pickup code.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's both topics settled. Thanks all, and let's open the doors.
